title: Freedom-to-operate DRAM built only from expired patents
idea: Ideal: technology with no owner. Closest achievable: design a DDR4/LPDDR4-compatible part using only expired-patent cell, stacked-capacitor and sense-amp techniques, backed by a formal freedom-to-operate audit, so an entrant faces no royalty stack or injunctions.
why: Entry barrier and cost: removes a ~3-5% royalty stack and injunction risk at some performance cost.

title: Domestic molybdenum wordlines replace Chinese tungsten
idea: Box[Material=Mo buried wordline and contacts x Source=U.S. Mo mines (by-product of Cu/Mo mining) x Fab=ALD Mo fill x Owner=mine-to-precursor offtake x Finance=DPA Title III]: qualify Mo (lower resistivity at narrow widths, no TiN liner) for buried wordlines and plugs, with a U.S. precursor supply chain under long-term offtake.
why: Removes the ~80% China tungsten chokepoint and lowers wordline RC; U.S. manufacturability of a critical material.

title: Rack-level weight broadcast: one copy of model weights, many accelerators
idea: Information theory says N identical copies carry the information of one, yet inference clusters replicate the same weights in every accelerator's HBM. Put a single weight copy in a CXL/optical multicast memory appliance per rack and stream tiles with deterministic prefetch, keeping only working tiles and KV-cache in local HBM.
why: Do DRAM's job with less: for 8-64-way replicated serving, cuts weight-holding HBM 4-30x, freeing HBM wafer capacity (3x area/bit tax) at the cost of a few extra pJ/bit of streaming.

title: Pure-play DRAM foundry serving fabless memory designers
idea: Rearrange IDM into foundry: a fab offers a DRAM process (cells, capacitors, buried wordline) as a service with a PDK. Fabless firms and hyperscalers then design their own arrays and periphery, with custom page sizes, banks and interfaces.
why: Spreads fab capital across many designers, raising utilization and design variety. Could create a fourth major supply source, as TSMC did for logic.

title: Block-copolymer self-assembly patterns capacitors, defects absorbed by codes
idea: Inverts 'every pillar must print perfectly': pattern the honeycomb storage-node array with directed self-assembly on a 193i guide pattern; DSA's notorious ~0.1-1% missing or merged pillars, long a blocker, now fall within the cell error budget.
why: EUV and masks: replaces 1-2 EUV or multi-patterning steps per wafer with a cheap spin-and-anneal step.

title: Salvage-binned DRAM: fuse off dead banks, sell lower capacity
idea: Inverts 'a die with a dead bank is scrap': map failing banks or channels, fuse them off, and sell 24 Gb parts from 32 Gb die or reduced-channel HBM stacks, the way GPUs are salvage-binned.
why: Yield and cost per bit: recovers a few percent of die now scrapped, especially on new nodes and in HBM where stack yield is down 20-30%.

title: RISC-V-style royalty-free DRAM patent pool and periphery generator
idea: Like RISC-V plus the MPEG-LA patent pool, a foundation assembles expired 6F2/8F2 cell, sense-amp and DLL patents with donated ones into a royalty-free pool and ships an open-source periphery compiler that generates JEDEC-compliant row/column logic for a given process.
why: Lowers the IP and design entry barrier (often $0.5-1B and years) for new DRAM makers, especially U.S. and allied entrants.

title: Exchange-traded DRAM bit futures for price discovery and hedging
idea: Ideal: memory prices known years ahead. Closest achievable: standardized cash-settled quarterly futures per Gb of DDR5-equivalent on an exchange (CME/LME style), letting buyers hedge and new fabs pre-sell output as collateral for lenders.
why: Capital cost: hedged revenue lowers WACC by several points and makes entrant fabs financeable.

title: All-solid-state 193 nm fiber-laser light source for DUV scanners
idea: Scale jump from a meter-long gas-discharge chamber to fiber photonics: frequency-convert a high-power Yb fiber laser array (fifth or sixth harmonic in nonlinear crystals) to 193 nm, so scanners need no neon buffer gas and no argon or krypton.
why: Excimer lasers consume neon, a chokepoint since 2022. This cuts the gas cost, frees DUV-based DRAM lines from rare-gas supply, and cuts laser maintenance.

title: Laser decap and rebump LPDDR die mined from e-waste phones
idea: Inverts 'e-waste recycling means shredding for gold': robotic lines laser-decapsulate package-on-package stacks from recycled phones, extract the LPDDR die, re-bump and retest them, and package them for IoT, automotive and edge boards.
why: Scarce resource and supply: billions of retired phones hold exabytes of working LPDDR silicon; even 10% recovery adds meaningful low-end supply at near-zero wafer cost.

title: Substitute EUV array patterning with block-copolymer self-assembly at 250 C
idea: Swap EUV for directed self-assembly of block copolymers (annealed at ~250 C) guided by coarse DUV templates, which naturally forms the periodic hexagonal and line arrays memory tiers need.
why: Breaks the single-supplier EUV chokepoint for array layers and cuts patterning cost per layer ~3x.

title: Open CXL reference controller for static and nonvolatile memories
idea: Worse: make each new memory maker build its own controller and survive hyperscaler qualification alone. Flip: an OCP-style consortium publishes open RTL and firmware for a CXL Type-3 controller with no refresh engine, persistence and wear hooks, and a shared qualification suite.
why: Cuts time-to-market for refresh-free memories by ~2 years and lowers entry cost.

title: No silicon wafer: substrate-neutral CHIPS grants paid per verified bit-capacity
idea: Forced limit: subsidies cannot favour Si. A grant tranche pays per verified Gb of monthly capacity added per dollar of capex, open to glass, foil, SiC and disk lines, with milestones audited by third-party benchmark.
why: Capital: steers public money to the cheapest bits per dollar rather than incumbent process paths.

title: Stripe codewords across many die to pool error budgets
idea: Inverts 'each DRAM die must stand on its own quality': a CXL controller interleaves every codeword across 8-16 die from mixed sources (harvested, reject, new), so a die near 1% raw BER is averaged with clean die and the code works at the pooled rate.
why: Reuse and yield: lets heterogeneous, imperfect die be pooled into reliable memory, widening what is sellable from every supply stream.

title: Curie-point magnetic taggants encode material recipe for automated recycling
idea: Mold compound and substrates carry a few mg of ferrite microparticles with chosen Curie temperatures (e.g. 60/90/120/150 C). A recycler sweeps magnetization against temperature to decode the bill of materials and die grade, then routes each part to reuse or the right refinery.
why: Manual sorting caps recovery; machine-readable composition raises reuse and recovery rates.

title: Cloud noisy-RAM tier for inference weights at a discount
idea: Inverts 'all memory bits must be equal': clouds sell a cheaper memory tier for model weights and KV caches on 1%-raw-BER DRAM; models get noise-injection fine-tuning, and sign and exponent bits sit in a small ECC-protected region.
why: Supply allocation: puts the largest new demand (AI inference) on memory that would otherwise be scrapped, freeing perfect DRAM elsewhere; ~20-40% lower cost per bit for that tier.

title: Svalbard-style shared die vault replacing last-time-buy hoarding
idea: Like a seed vault, an industry cooperative stores Grade-1 qualified DRAM wafers sealed in dry nitrogen at low temperature, then packages and 125 C-screens die on demand for members, so OEMs stop each holding 5-10x over-buys for 10-year programs.
why: Pooling long-life inventory across OEMs cuts hoarded industrial/automotive DRAM 50-70%, releasing that supply to the market.

title: DRAM refinery re-bins decommissioned server DIMMs into CXL capacity
idea: First principle: DRAM has no intrinsic wear-out (no tunnel-oxide damage as in flash), so a 5-year-old server DIMM's cells are physically almost as good as new. Regional refineries pull retired DDR4/DDR5 at hyperscaler decommission, run 48-hour retention and pattern screens, re-bin at relaxed timing, and remount modules or dies onto CXL Type-3 expander cards for capacity-tier memory.
why: Usable supply and cost per bit: hyperscalers retire on the order of 10^8 GB/yr; recapturing ~30% adds several percent to global usable supply at ~10-20% of new-bit cost, with near-zero capital or scarce-resource intensity.

title: Reinsurance-backed 10-year 125 C warranty bonds for new entrants
idea: Like contractor surety bonds, reinsurers underwrite a 10-year 125 C field-failure warranty on memory from new suppliers, priced from HTOL data and fleet telemetry, so automakers can buy from untested fabs with the risk transferred.
why: Removes the incumbency barrier in automotive memory (where buyers fear newcomers), letting new U.S. capacity sell premium parts years earlier.

title: Privateer's letter of marque: advance market commitment for U.S. DRAM
idea: Governments once licensed privateers with guaranteed prize money. Here the U.S. issues an advance market commitment: federal datacenters and DoD will buy the first 2 EB of U.S.-made DRAM that meets a spec, at a guaranteed $/GB floor for 5 years, from any entrant.
why: Demand-side de-risking for U.S. manufacturability: guaranteed offtake makes new entrants bankable without the government picking technology winners.

title: Silicon-carbide access transistors make refresh-free DRAM in U.S. power fabs
idea: Junction and off-state leakage scale with intrinsic carrier density n_i ~ exp(-Eg/2kT); 4H-SiC (3.26 eV) has n_i ~1e-9 cm^-3, about 1e18 below Si, so retention moves from milliseconds to hours. Build 1T1C arrays on 200 mm SiC lines (already operating in the U.S.) using only SiC, SiO2, Al, Zr and TiN.
why: Refresh wall and U.S. manufacturability: eliminates refresh (16-33% of idle power) using domestic SiC capacity; risks are SiC/SiO2 interface traps, low channel mobility and ~3x wafer cost.

title: Put SiC fab overcapacity to work on wide-bandgap, near-refresh-free DRAM
idea: Downhole and EV users built SiC fabs that now have spare capacity. 4H-SiC's 3.2 eV bandgap cuts storage-node leakage so far that 1990s SiC DRAM cells held charge for hours; build SiC-MOS 1T1C arrays on underused U.S. SiC lines for refresh-free memory tiers.
why: Attacks refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) and U.S. supply with idle 150/200 mm SiC lines; density is far lower, so it starts in niche or slow tiers.

title: Rotary-press ALD: spatial gas-zone heads for capacitor high-k
idea: A rotary press inks paper as it runs past fixed rollers. A spatial-ALD head with alternating precursor and purge slots, machined and assembled in a university shop, sweeps wafers under fixed gas zones at atmospheric pressure. It deposits ZrO2/HfO2/Al2O3 capacitor stacks 10-50x faster than temporal ALD.
why: Capital and tool count: high-k ALD is a large tool-count item, and spatial heads cut ALD capex per wafer start several-fold. An open design spreads to micro-fabs.

title: Spinning-jenny probe cards: MEMS cantilever arrays testing every die at once
idea: The spinning jenny let one worker run dozens of spindles. Fabricate MEMS probe cards in a nanofab: electroplated Ni-Co cantilevers on silicon at ~40 um pitch, so one touchdown contacts every die on the wafer for parallel retention and row-hammer screening.
why: Test capital is ~10-15% of DRAM cost and a capacity choke: one-touch whole-wafer test cuts tester count ~5x and frees floor space.

title: ETA-10 Revival: Liquid-Nitrogen Pods for Commodity DRAM at 77 K
idea: Revive ETA Systems' 1987 liquid-nitrogen-immersed CMOS supercomputer: immerse standard DRAM in LN2 pods (nitrogen is abundant, unlike helium), where leakage collapses so retention reaches minutes and refresh is switched off, the steeper subthreshold slope lets VARY and wordline drop to ~0.4/1.2 V, and copper resistance falls ~7x.
why: Energy per access: V2 cut ~6-8x, wire RC ~7x lower, refresh gone, net ~10x lower energy per access; also returns the 10-20% of bandwidth lost to refresh, using existing chips and a new packaging business.

title: Eliminate equity-funded fabs: take-or-pay prepayments collateralize fab bonds
idea: Eliminate funding fabs from equity at the cycle top: hyperscalers sign 7-10-year take-or-pay bit contracts that, like LNG offtake agreements, collateralize project-finance bonds for a dedicated US fab SPV.
why: Lowers cost of capital ~3-5 points on a $15B fab where depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost.

title: Homogeneity: deep-trench eDRAM built into passive silicon interposers
idea: TRIZ #33 Homogeneity: silicon interposers already made at 65 nm on plentiful lines get one added deep-trench capacitor mask (plus existing transistor flow where available) to carry GB-scale eDRAM in otherwise passive silicon under the accelerator.
why: Supply and data movement: moves some HBM demand onto under-used interposer capacity with short wires.

title: Eliminate the patent thicket: public commons from distressed DRAM portfolios
idea: Eliminate royalty barriers: a public-private fund buys DRAM patent portfolios from exited or bankrupt players and licenses them royalty-free to any US-made memory entrant, with pooled defensive countersuit rights.
why: Removes litigation risk that deters new DRAM entrants; one portfolio buy can protect a dozen startups.

title: Prospector reworks tailings: tungsten from fab waste and boards
idea: Like prospectors reworking old tailings, recover tungsten from WF6 exhaust scrubbers, W-CMP slurry and scrapped memory boards by electrochemical leaching and solvent extraction. The output is domestic fab-grade WF6 feedstock.
why: Scarce-resource chokepoint (China ~80% of tungsten): well under half of the WF6 fed into a chamber ends up as film, so a closed loop could cover a large share of a U.S. DRAM fab's tungsten demand.

title: Double-blind inventory clearinghouse to kill DRAM bullwhip hoarding
idea: Po: every warehouse is made of glass. A neutral party collects encrypted inventory and order data from DRAM makers, distributors and top buyers and, via secure multiparty computation, publishes only weekly aggregate true-demand and channel-inventory indices (like JODI for oil).
why: Double-ordering and hoarding amplify a ~10-15% supply gap into a 4x price spike; transparency deflates phantom demand and lets fabs plan capacity; attacks effective supply.

title: Zero new dies for 24 months: robotic chip-level DIMM reclamation
idea: Self-imposed limit: no fresh dies allowed. Robotic lines desolder DRAM packages from retired hyperscaler DIMMs, reball, retest and speed-bin each die, then remount them on CXL Type-3 expanders whose controller trains per-die timing so mixed-speed reclaimed DDR4/DDR5 dies run as one pool.
why: Supply/reuse: retired fleets discard tens of millions of working GB a year; recovering 30-50% of it adds several percent to usable bit supply at ~$1/GB rework cost with zero wafer starts.

title: Eliminate photomasks: multi-beam direct write for low-volume DRAM
idea: Eliminate $10-30M mask sets for small-lot memory: multi-beam e-beam writers expose critical layers directly for specialty DRAM (rad-hard, automotive, custom HBM base dies), allowing per-wafer design changes.
why: Removes mask capital as a barrier to new entrants; throughput is low but adequate for <1k wafers/month niches.

title: Pay-per-exposure EUV scanners as securitized tool-as-a-service
idea: Box[Finance=scanner owned by lessor SPV, metered per wafer-layer exposure x Owner=tool vendor + asset managers x Scale=any fab]: lithography scanners are owned by an asset-backed vehicle and billed per exposure, moving ~$200M-per-tool capex off DRAM makers' balance sheets.
why: Capital intensity and depreciation (~55% of wafer cost): turns fixed cost into variable cost and lowers new-entrant barriers.

title: Open patent pool for abundant-element process substitutions
idea: Qualification cost scales with test-hours, not with the number of fabs, yet every fab re-qualifies substitutes alone and patents are scattered. A government-seeded pool licenses all abundant-element substitutions (TiN for W, ZrO2 for HfO2, Zn-Si-O for IGZO) FRAND at a flat per-wafer fee and publishes shared HTOL and retention data.
why: Scarce-resource intensity and U.S. manufacturability: shared reliability data cuts qualification time and cost, accelerating banned-element exit by years.

title: Water-gated subsidies: full award only at one-tenth liters per bit
idea: Reverse incentive design: memory subsidies and permits are tiered by verified liters of fresh water per GB shipped, with the full award only at 10% of today's industry baseline. Overperformers earn tradable water-per-bit credits.
why: Water turns from a siting obstacle into a competitive axis. The rule pulls dry processes and reuse into new U.S. fabs and targets a 10x cut in industry water intensity.

title: Synthetic-silica crucibles from ordinary sand via chloride purification
idea: Worse: depend on Spruce Pine quartz for every crystal puller. Flip: convert common silica sand to SiCl4, distill it, and hydrolyze it into synthetic fused-silica grain for crucible inner layers, then regenerate used crucibles by stripping and re-lining only the inner layer.
why: Breaks a >80% single-mine dependency for crucibles; scarce-resource intensity of wafers drops.

title: Arrhenius cold-grade bin turns retention fallout into sellable memory
idea: Junction leakage roughly doubles every ~10 C, so a die that fails 64 ms retention at 85 C has ~16x margin at 45 C. Create a JEDEC 'cold-grade' bin and SPD flag for dies that pass only below 50 C, sold exclusively into liquid- and immersion-cooled AI racks that guarantee die temperature.
why: Recovers the 3-8% of wafer output scrapped or down-binned for retention, raising bit supply with zero new fab capital; refresh energy also drops in those racks.

title: Fe: Fe/Cr coupled antiferromagnet removes iridium and ruthenium from MRAM
idea: Replace Ru-spacer synthetic antiferromagnets and IrMn/PtMn pinning in MTJ stacks with Fe/Cr interlayer-coupled multilayers and a high-anisotropy Fe-based reference layer.
why: Ir and Ru are among the scarcest elements; removing them lets non-volatile MRAM scale to commodity volume.

title: Minify speed, magnify bins: JEDEC DDR-Slow capacity grade
idea: Standardize a JEDEC grade with ~2x relaxed timings and refresh (e.g. 256 ms window at low temperature) that accepts speed- and retention-failed bins from any node and lets old lines qualify, targeted at CXL capacity tiers.
why: Turns speed/retention fallout into sellable product and creates demand for older nodes; adds ~5-15% usable bits per wafer.

title: Eliminate software bloat: memory-footprint bounties for top open-source apps
idea: Eliminate wasted bytes: a $1M bounty fund pays per verified MB saved, times installed base, for merged patches that cut resident memory in Chromium, Electron, Firefox, Kubernetes components and JVM defaults, measured on a public benchmark.
why: A 10% cut in browser/Electron memory across billions of devices frees hundreds of PB of effective capacity and delays RAM upgrades.

title: Orbital Hall torques in titanium make chokepoint-free MRAM a foundry add-on
idea: Light metals like Ti and Cr show a large orbital Hall effect that can switch a magnetic free layer like spin Hall torque does, without beta-W or Pt. The SOT-MRAM stack is sputter-only BEOL, so any U.S. logic foundry can add a refresh-free, ns-class memory tier.
why: Adds DRAM-class capacity in existing fabs while avoiding tungsten and platinum-group metals; no refresh power.

title: Bi: Bismuth-antimony topological SOT-MRAM from HDD reader know-how
idea: Use sputtered BiSb, with a record spin Hall angle developed for HDD readers, as the spin-orbit-torque write line in MRAM instead of W, Ta or Pt.
why: ~10x lower write current than W-based SOT and avoids China-dominated tungsten and platinum.

title: Nanoimprint memory litho with siloxane-brush non-fluorinated release
idea: Fuse Canon-style nanoimprint lithography (already qualified for memory pitches) with a PDMS/siloxane polymer-brush or graphene release layer on the quartz template, replacing the fluorinated FOTS anti-stick monolayer.
why: Gives an EUV-free, PFAS-free patterning route at about 1/10 the litho capex of EUV for DRAM array layers.

title: No silicon wafer: laser-lift-off memory foils laminated onto packages
idea: Forced limit: no thick substrate. Oxide-TFT memory tiers are built on polyimide on a reusable glass carrier, released with flexible-OLED laser lift-off, and laminated as micron-thin memory foils onto logic packages.
why: Uses the large flexible-OLED LLO base. The carrier is reused, and thin foils stack without TSVs, avoiding the HBM TSV tax.

title: Airline overbooking: statistically overcommitted DRAM with bump pool
idea: Like airlines selling 105% of seats, cloud providers sell VMs with 130% of physical DRAM, backed by an actuarial model of peak co-usage and a 'bump pool' of compressed and CXL-attached memory that absorbs overflow, with credits paid when a tenant is bumped.
why: Buyers purchase 20-25% less DRAM per sold GB; the bump-pool tier costs far less per bit.

title: Minify copies to one: optical broadcast weight streaming
idea: Keep one copy of model weights in a central memory pool and broadcast it over a WDM optical bus to 128 accelerators in lockstep; each holds only a tiny SRAM double-buffer and pipelines layer by layer as weights stream past.
why: Eliminates per-accelerator weight replicas (most HBM capacity), cutting physical memory per served model ~100x at the cost of synchronized batch scheduling.

title: Own zero EUV: tolling critical layers at a partner scanner
idea: Self-imposed limit: no EUV ownership. A DUV-only DRAM fab ships sealed, nitrogen-purged FOUPs to a partner's EUV cell for only the 1-2 layers where multipatterning is uneconomic, paying per exposure.
why: Capital intensity: avoids $200M+ per scanner and its single-supplier queue while keeping 1b-class density.

title: Food time-temperature indicator as on-die Arrhenius life odometer
idea: Like time-temperature labels on vaccines, each die integrates temperature x time through an always-on leakage-to-counter circuit that reports consumed life at 125 C equivalent, letting buyers price used memory like mileage on a car.
why: Enables a trusted secondary market for long-life memory, raising reuse rates and lowering qualification risk; adds <0.1% die area.

title: Effective-GB compressed CXL modules sold with capacity warranty
idea: Combine inline hardware LZ4/zstd compression and a deduplication engine with a commercial guarantee: the vendor sells 'effective GB' and warrants 2× capacity on qualified workloads, with telemetry and true-up credits.
why: Doubles usable capacity per physical bit for compressible data. The warranty turns a technical trick into procurement-grade supply.

title: Power-by-the-hour: lease memory bits, take modules back, redeploy
idea: Rolls-Royce sells engine thrust-hours, not engines. Memory makers keep ownership of modules and bill per GB-hour, with telemetry from the SPD/CXL controller. Modules are reclaimed, re-screened and redeployed across customers as one fleet over 2-3 service lives.
why: Usable supply: lifetime bit-hours per wafer rise ~1.5-2x and shortages smooth out. Makers gain aftermarket revenue that funds new capacity.

title: Ramtron's PZT exile solved: FeRAM in inkjet piezo-MEMS fabs
idea: Ramtron's PZT ferroelectric RAM stayed niche partly because PZT and Pt/Ir electrodes contaminate CMOS lines, which forced a segregated module. Piezo-MEMS fabs that make inkjet heads and sensors already run PZT/Pt/Ir on 200 mm with 1990s-class tools: put the ferroelectric capacitor module there, on top of 0.35-0.18 um CMOS wafers.
why: Opens a non-DRAM fab pool for refresh-free 1T1C ferroelectric memory to replace legacy DRAM and battery-backed SRAM in industrial and automotive uses, freeing commodity DRAM; PZT endurance (~10^12-10^15) is the limit.

title: Eliminate factory final test: in-field BIST screening and soft repair
idea: Eliminate long DRAM final test and burn-in: dies ship after short wafer sort, carrying on-die BIST and soft post-package repair, and finish retention and pattern screening inside the customer's system during the first weeks of operation.
why: Test is ~10-15% of DRAM cost and ATE is a capacity bottleneck; cutting test time raises output throughput ~20-30% with existing testers.

title: Five-minute electricity-style spot market for pooled CXL memory
idea: Adapted from grid operators' 5-minute real-time dispatch: rack-level CXL memory pools post free GB every 5 minutes into an internal auction. Tenants bid by latency tier, and the hypervisor migrates pages to the winners, with locational prices for near and far pools.
why: Clouds strand ~25-50% of provisioned DRAM; marginal pricing pushes utilization toward ~80% and cuts DRAM bought per workload ~20-30% (usable supply).

title: Power-by-the-hour DRAM leasing with manufacturer take-back
idea: Like Rolls-Royce leasing jet-engine thrust-hours, memory makers keep ownership of modules, bill per GB-hour from on-module telemetry, and take modules back at end of term for retest and redeployment in lower tiers.
why: Aligns the maker with lifetime utilization, closes the reuse loop and smooths revenue; extends average module service life from ~4 to ~8 years.

title: Substitute factory burn-in ovens with in-host self-burn-in
idea: Swap long ATE/oven burn-in for shipping modules after short screens and running a 72-hour on-board BIST burn-in inside the customer's server at first boot, reporting telemetry and remapping weak rows before production use.
why: Burn-in/test capacity bottlenecks output; shifting it to the host frees ~30-50% of test-floor capacity and shortens cycle time by days.

title: Delete spare rows, fuses and laser repair from the die
idea: Inverts 'arrays need redundancy and repair': design die with no spare rows or columns, no e-fuse banks and no repair test insertion; scattered faults up to 1% are handled by a host-side defect map and coding.
why: Periphery area and test capital: frees ~3-5% of die area and a full tester insertion, raising die per wafer and tester throughput.

title: NEC 4-Level DRAM Revival With Setun Balanced-Ternary Storage
idea: Revive NEC's 1997 four-level 4 Gb DRAM and the Soviet Setun's balanced-ternary memory: store three levels (-, 0, +) around the VDD/2 bitline precharge so the 0 state needs no charge, sensed by a two-step sense amplifier with a reference half-cell, giving 1.58 bits per cell on an unchanged capacitor.
why: Density and cost per bit: ~58% more bits per wafer on existing fabs without new litho; only two thresholds are sensed, easing the 5 fF charge wall versus 4-level designs.

title: Putting-out system: idle academic cleanrooms do paid value-add steps
idea: Under the 18th-century putting-out system, merchants sent cloth to cottage workshops. Memory makers ship die-banked or reclaimed dies to U.S. university nanofabs for off-hour value-add work that needs only aligners, evaporators and bonders (redistribution layers, micro-bumping, re-sort), paying per finished piece.
why: Capacity and U.S. manufacturability: ~100 U.S. academic cleanrooms run at ~30-50% utilization. Selling idle hours adds specialty packaging supply and funds the fabs.

title: Laser-decap and reball LPDDR die from discarded phones and laptops
idea: A GB of DRAM is ~42 mg of silicon whose value is entirely in its pattern, and discarded phones carry working LPDDR. Automated lines X-ray-locate PoP packages, laser-ablate mold compound, extract die, test them on a carrier, and rebuild them as fan-out packages for embedded, IoT and low-end PC markets.
why: Supply and scarce resources: ~1.2 billion phones/yr x 4-8 GB is several EB of DRAM entering e-waste (~20% of annual output); recovering 10% adds ~2% global supply with little capital.

title: Ramtron EDRAM/Mitsubishi CDRAM: SRAM Row Cache on Every DRAM Bank
idea: Revive the 1990s Enhanced DRAM and Cached DRAM, which put SRAM row caches beside each bank: a 2-4 row SRAM cache per subarray serves repeated hits (hot KV heads, embedding rows) with no activation and lets the DRAM row close at once, reducing activations that also drive row hammer.
why: Hits cost ~0.2-0.5 pJ/bit versus ~5.9 pJ per useful bit for activate-read-restore, ~10x on hit-heavy AI traffic; fabbed on existing DRAM processes.

title: Bottle-deposit refunds on every gigabyte of DRAM
idea: Po: memory has a bottle deposit. A refundable deposit (e.g., $0.50/GB) is charged on DRAM-bearing devices and modules and refunded when they are returned to a certified harvester; unclaimed deposits fund harvest-plant capex.
why: Bottle-bill regions see 70-90% return rates versus ~20% e-waste collection; guarantees predictable feedstock so die/package harvesting can be financed; attacks scarce-resource intensity and supply.

title: Local quality: lifetime-matched retention binning for short-lived AI data
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: instead of one 64 ms retention spec, bin dies by measured retention (8/16/32/64 ms) and sell fast-leaking dies into streaming buffers, activation scratchpads and NIC queues where data is overwritten before it decays; the controller refresh rate is read from the die's bin fuse.
why: Retention tail (fact 3) currently scraps or downgrades dies; matching data lifetime to retention adds ~3-6% sellable output.

title: K: KOH crystallographic etch digs ultra-high-aspect capacitor trenches
idea: On (110) silicon, anisotropic KOH/TMAH etching exposes vertical {111} sidewalls with >100:1 rate selectivity, so hardmask-defined trenches reach AR >100 on cheap wet benches instead of cryogenic plasma HAR etchers.
why: Fact #1 needs AR ~115; wet benches cost ~1/10 of HAR etch tools and relieve the etch-tool bottleneck.

title: Buyer cooperative co-owns a fab and takes bits at cost
idea: Electricity co-ops proved users can own capital-heavy plants. OEMs, clouds and automakers buy equity in a memory co-op fab in proportion to their offtake and receive bits at cost-plus, removing the producer margin that balloons during shortages.
why: Cost per bit in shortages: members pay depreciation plus opex instead of 4x contract prices, and guaranteed offtake de-risks the financing.

title: Vinyl-record stamping: nanoimprint masters for repetitive array layers
idea: Like pressing records from one master, use nanoimprint templates for the highly periodic bitline, storage-node and landing-pad layers, keeping EUV only for irregular periphery layers; templates are cloned from an e-beam master in a domestic mask shop.
why: Removes 3-4 of 5-7 EUV layers, easing the single-supplier EUV chokepoint and cutting litho capex and energy per wafer by ~30-40%.

title: Downhole-oil HT-SOI lines retooled for hot automotive DRAM
idea: Like the 200 C SOI electronics used in oil wells, put DRAM cells on thick buried oxide so the storage-node junction has no bulk leakage path, made on existing 200 mm HT-SOI fabs that already qualify parts for 10 years at 125-175 C.
why: Junction-leakage-limited retention at 125 C improves ~5-10x, cutting hot refresh, while moving auto bits onto otherwise niche U.S./EU lines.

title: All-electrochemical metallization replacing argon sputter PVD
idea: Molecule-by-molecule wiring: ALD seeds, then electroless Co/Ni and electroplated Cu/Ru for contacts, bit lines and the back end, plus reactive pure-N2 deposition for TiN electrodes, so no argon-sputter PVD chamber is needed.
why: PVD is the main argon user in a DRAM fab. Wet metallization tools also cost ~50% less per wafer pass and run at atmospheric pressure.

title: Diatom-grown biosilica as high-purity quartz for crucibles
idea: Diatoms build glass shells from dissolved silica at room temperature. Diatoms grown in photobioreactors on purified silicic acid yield biosilica that is calcined, acid-polished and fused into synthetic high-purity quartz for Czochralski crucibles.
why: Breaks the Spruce Pine >80% high-purity quartz chokepoint for silicon crystal growth.

title: Mask-free interference lithography for the periodic DRAM array layers
idea: A DRAM array is a periodic lattice whose information content is a few numbers (pitch, angle, phase); encoding it in a $1M mask and EUV photons is overkill. Expose the dense array layers with multi-beam 193 nm immersion interference or achromatic Talbot lithography, using a conventional scanner only for the cut, trim and array-edge layers.
why: EUV chokepoint and capital: removes 3-5 EUV layers with tools ~10x cheaper per layer; the risk is overlay of cut layers to the interference grating and edge defects.

title: Inversion: mask-frozen DRAM nodes depreciated over 15 years
idea: TRIZ #13 Inversion: stop node migration; freeze a DRAM node's mask set for 15 years and allow just one added mask per generation for incremental gains (e.g., a second capacitor tier), so tools fully depreciate before replacement.
why: Depreciation ~55% of wafer cost: stretching tool life from 5 to 15 years cuts cost per bit more than a node shrink's 10-20%.

title: Cross-tenant memory exchange points in colocation campuses
idea: Po: memory is a utility traded between strangers. Like an Internet exchange point, a neutral CXL 3.x switch fabric in each colo lets tenants post idle DRAM and others lease it by the GB-hour, with per-lease memory-encryption keys and bandwidth QoS enforced in the switch.
why: Fleet studies show ~25-50% of server DRAM stranded; turning 10% of it into tradeable supply equals a new fab's annual output; attacks effective cost per bit and capital.

title: Minify the vacuum: atmospheric mist-CVD oxide memory fab
idea: Deposit IGZO/Ga2O3 channels and high-k capacitor oxides by atmospheric mist CVD and solution combustion synthesis, pattern with atmospheric-plasma etch, and eliminate vacuum chambers, load locks and turbopumps in a warehouse-grade fab.
why: Vacuum hardware is a large share of tool cost and energy; vacuum-free layers at ~$5-20/m2 each, stacked 16-32 high, target ~100x lower $/GB, accepting lower mobility and slower cells.

title: Substitute DRAM fabs with idle display panel fabs making oxide memory
idea: Swap new DRAM fabs for under-used Gen-8.5 LCD/OLED lines, whose IGZO backplane processes already stay below ~350-400 C, upgraded with sub-um panel steppers to make 2T0C oxide gain-cell memory dies on glass.
why: Uses tens of billions of dollars of depreciated capacity for slower-capacity memory tiers; density per area is far lower, so the gain is capital and time-to-supply, not cost per bit.

title: Venus-flytrap snap-through NEMS latches built in idle MEMS fabs
idea: The flytrap stores a state as one of two buckled leaf shapes and snaps between them. Pre-buckled nanobeams with two stable curvatures are switched electrostatically and read through a tunneling gap or a gated FET under the beam, using the release-etch processes U.S. MEMS fabs already run.
why: Uses underloaded MEMS capacity, with zero standby power and no refresh, capacitor or EUV.

title: Inert atmosphere: sealed-pod minimal-fab makes DRAM inside ordinary warehouses
idea: TRIZ #39 Inert atmosphere: every wafer stays in nitrogen-filled pods docked to sealed tool minienvironments, so a fixed legacy DRAM flow plus at most one new mask runs in a standard warehouse without a ballroom cleanroom.
why: Capital and distributed U.S. manufacturing: cleanroom building cost falls by most of its share.

title: Salmon-homing take-back: deposit-refund chip ID for DRAM modules
idea: Salmon return to the river they hatched in. Each module carries a cryptographic ID and a deposit built into its price, refunded when it comes back through the vendor's reverse-logistics network, which routes it to test, redeployment or die harvesting.
why: Raises module recovery from <20% to >80%, as bottle bills do, feeding second-life supply.

title: Buyer-owned memory cooperative fab, Ocean-Spray style
idea: Combine agricultural co-op ownership with a DRAM fab. Tier-2 clouds, automakers, PC OEMs and defense primes buy member shares in proportion to their volume and receive output at cost plus a reserve, with patronage dividends when prices spike.
why: Members swap price exposure for capex ownership. It aligns long-term demand with supply and opens a new buyer-funded U.S. capacity channel outside the three incumbents.

title: Magnify the cache ratio 128:1: flash-backed DRAM-class memory
idea: Present SLC 3D NAND as byte-addressable memory through a controller with a DRAM cache 1/128 of capacity, write coalescing, hot-page prediction and terabyte-wide wear leveling; NAND is written only on eviction, so endurance holds by architecture.
why: Blended cost ~ NAND ~$0.06/GB + 0.8% DRAM = ~$0.15/GB, ~100x cheaper, trading tail latency (microseconds on misses) for capacity.

title: Magnify the substrate 100x: Gen-10.5 display fabs make memory
idea: Repurpose overbuilt Gen-10.5 LCD/OLED backplane lines (2.9 x 3.4 m glass) to deposit 16-32 stacked layers of IGZO 2T0C gain cells at a 0.5-1 um rule, with periphery on small CMOS chiplets bonded along tile edges; panels are diced into memory tiles.
why: Processed panel cost is ~$100-300/m2 per layer stack vs ~$80,000/m2 for DRAM wafers; even at ~1/20 DRAM bit density, cost targets ~$0.1/GB (~100x cheaper), accepting ~100-300 ns access and frequent refresh.

title: Al: U.S. BAW-filter fabs make aluminum-boron-nitride ferroelectric memory
idea: RF BAW filter fabs already sputter piezoelectric AlN at volume; adding boron co-sputtering yields wurtzite Al(1-x)B(x)N ferroelectric (Pr >100 uC/cm2) capacitors and FeFETs as a BEOL non-volatile memory.
why: Abundant Al, B, N replace scarce Sc of AlScN and reuse existing U.S. sputter capacity; huge Pr allows tiny cells.

title: No silicon wafer: idle Gen 8.5 LCD fabs make oxide-TFT memory panels
idea: Forced limit: no Si wafers. Convert overbuilt Gen 8.5 LCD backplane fabs (2.2x2.5 m glass, about 70x the area of a 300 mm wafer) to make IGZO 2T gain-cell arrays at about 1 um rules, sold as a slow-DRAM capacity tier.
why: Capital and supply: reuses stranded display capacity worth tens of billions; about 30 GB per panel per tier, near parity at shortage prices for a capacity tier.

title: Carbon-mandrel inverse damascene for fluorine-free contact holes
idea: Combine amorphous-carbon pillars (patterned with O2 plasma) with conformal low-temperature oxide fill and CMP. The carbon mandrels are then ashed out in O2, leaving contact or storage-node holes in oxide without ever etching oxide.
why: Replaces fluorocarbon high-AR oxide etch with O2 ash, which is F-free and cheaper per step, and makes PFAS-free DRAM contacts possible.

title: Tile-architecture dies that survive wafer-edge truncation
idea: Edge case on the wafer itself: partial reticle shots at the rim are scrapped. Lay out DRAM as independently addressed tiles, each with its own I/O hub tap, so a truncated edge die still works as a half- or quarter-capacity part binned as a lower-density SKU.
why: Recovers ~3-6% of 300 mm wafer area as sellable bits with no new tools.

title: Taking out: move DRAM periphery to foundry wafers, hybrid-bond back
idea: TRIZ #2 Extraction: strip sense amps, decoders and I/O off the DRAM wafer so the scarce DRAM fab prints only cell arrays, while plentiful logic foundries build the periphery wafer; the two are joined by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding at 1-2 um pitch.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die: ~1.6-1.9x more bits per scarce DRAM wafer start, and periphery gets faster logic transistors.

title: Bottle-bill deposits on DRAM packages to fund reverse logistics
idea: Ideal: memory comes back by itself. Closest achievable: a $3-10 refundable deposit on every device's DRAM, redeemable at e-waste collectors who route memory packages to reprocessors, so the deposit pays for the collection network.
why: Reuse supply: collection of retired devices rises from ~20% to ~70%.

title: Conversion credits that turn idle U.S. logic fab modules into DRAM
idea: Ideal: memory capacity that already exists on U.S. soil. Closest achievable: a 40% tax credit plus a 7-year offtake guarantee for converting existing U.S. 300mm 45-65 nm logic modules to DRAM with ArFi multipatterning and refurbished capacitor tools, with no new shell or permitting.
why: U.S. share from 1-2% toward 4-5% in ~3 years at ~1/3 greenfield capex.

title: Dual-Port VRAM Revival: Serial Access Port Streams Entire DRAM Rows
idea: Revive the 1980s video RAM serial access memory (SAM) port: each bank gets a row-wide shift register that captures a full 8 KB row in one activation and streams it out through a narrow low-swing port, so weight and KV streams use 100% of each opened row instead of one 64 B burst.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): a random read costs ~5.9 pJ per useful bit because of 128x overfetch; consuming whole rows cuts activation energy per useful bit 50-100x and total access energy ~10x; buildable on existing DDR4/DDR5 lines with periphery changes only.

title: Substitute mined indium with indium recovered from scrapped LCD panels
idea: Swap primary indium (China ~60% of refining) for indium leached from e-waste LCD/ITO glass by acid recovery and electrowinning, feeding IGZO/ITO sputter targets for <=400 C oxide memory tiers.
why: Removes an emerging chokepoint for oxide-semiconductor memory; e-waste displays hold enough indium for many fabs' targets.

title: Resurrect IBM trench eDRAM at GlobalFoundries as U.S. memory chiplets
idea: Rearrange a logic foundry's role: restart the deep-trench-capacitor eDRAM modules GlobalFoundries inherited from IBM (used in POWER/z chips at 32/22/14 nm). Use them to make standalone DRAM-class cache and memory chiplets in New York as a domestic second source.
why: U.S. manufacturability: trench capacitors (~20 fF class) are already proven and no new fab capex is needed. The chiplets serve L4/near-memory demand that now consumes HBM and DRAM.

title: Strong oxidants: ozone leaching recovers tungsten from fab waste streams
idea: TRIZ #38 Strong oxidants: ozone/peroxide oxidative leaching recovers tungsten from CVD-W chamber cleans, CMP slurry and scrap wafers as tungstate, refined back to WF6 on-site; no lithography mask is added at all.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%): closes part of the loop for buried wordlines and contacts.

title: Cold-spray refill of sputter targets keeps scarce metal in the loop
idea: W, Ru and Ta rotary targets are designed with a thick reusable backing tube; eroded racetracks are refilled by cold spray, where powder bonds through adiabatic shear instability at ~800 m/s without melting.
why: Raises effective metal utilization from ~35% to >90% and cuts tungsten purchases.

title: Asymmetry: hyperscaler capex prepay for capped-price capacity call options
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry in risk-sharing: hyperscalers prepay ~30% of a new fab's capex and in return hold call options on 50% of its output at a capped price for 10 years, while the maker keeps all upside on the other half and all downside protection on the first.
why: Capital intensity and 3-5 year fab lag: de-risks greenfield builds so they start 1-2 years earlier during shortages.

title: Ant-trail data-in-motion: activations stream, never parked in DRAM
idea: Ant trails hold information in moving traffic and evaporating pheromone, not in a warehouse. Accelerators are scheduled so intermediate activations circulate through chip-to-chip pipeline links and are consumed before they ever need to be parked in DRAM.
why: Cuts DRAM/HBM capacity per AI inference system by ~30-50%, with no capacitor anywhere.

title: Phyllotaxis self-assembly patterns vertical-channel gain cell arrays
idea: Plants pack seeds and leaves in dense spirals through local inhibition. Block-copolymer directed self-assembly forms hexagonal arrays of ~10 nm-pitch vertical channel holes for vertical capacitorless transistors, guided by a sparse coarse pre-pattern.
why: Gets near-EUV density from chemistry, with ~3-4F2 hexagonal packing and no capacitor.

title: Crowe Cell Revival on SkyWater's U.S. Superconducting Process
idea: Revive J.W. Crowe's 1957 persistent-current cell, a bit stored as a circulating supercurrent in a niobium loop, on the 200 mm niobium superconducting processes already run in U.S. foundries, read by SQUIDs, to build attojoule-access memory banks for cryogenic AI and quantum data centers.
why: Energy per access ~1000x lower at chip level (aJ-fJ), still ~10x lower after cryocooler overhead; made in U.S. fabs with 250 nm-class litho and no EUV.

title: RAM-mileage standard: GB-per-request ratings in public procurement
idea: Ideal: software that needs no memory at all. Closest achievable: an Energy-Star-style rating of memory footprint (GB-seconds per transaction or per token) required in government and hyperscaler procurement, with annual CAFE-like improvement targets.
why: Usable supply from the demand side: 15-30% footprint cut from software bloat equals a new fab's output.
